title: Corporate Healthcare: The Wellness Apparatus
body:
Healthcare in GLMZ's corporate zones is simultaneously the most genuinely valuable benefit the corporate system provides and one of its most effective instruments of control. Major corporations operate comprehensive medical facilities within their zone territories, staffed by full-time physicians, specialists, and neural interface technicians whose employment is contingent on maintaining confidentiality protocols that run contrary to conventional medical ethics norms: patient records within corporate healthcare systems are classified as corporate operational data, accessible to HR and security divisions under the same zone sovereignty frameworks that govern other internal information. The doctor-patient privilege that exists in Meridian's municipal healthcare system does not apply in corporate medical facilities. Employees are informed of this in their induction documents. Most do not fully register the implication until they are already dependent on the system.

The quality of care available in corporate healthcare facilities is, for most employees, genuinely superior to what they could access through the tiered municipal system. Diagnostic capabilities are extensive, wait times are minimal, and the integration with employees' neural interfaces allows for continuous health monitoring that enables early detection of conditions that would go unnoticed in a conventional care model. The Nakamura-Osei Group's medical division has published internal data showing that employees in their residential zones have a 23% lower incidence of late-stage chronic disease diagnosis compared to demographically equivalent populations in unaffiliated zones — a statistic the corporation uses extensively in recruitment materials. The statistic is accurate. It omits the corresponding data showing that employee health data is routinely reviewed by HR algorithms flagging patterns associated with reduced productivity or increased leave likelihood.

Mental health services within the corporate wellness apparatus deserve particular examination. Every major corporation offers what it calls a 'psychological support program' — a combination of on-demand counseling, stress management tools delivered through neural interface, and crisis intervention services. These programs are widely used, particularly among employees in high-pressure technical and managerial roles. The counselors staffing them are licensed professionals. They are also corporate employees whose session records are technically protected by a confidentiality framework that explicitly excludes information classified as relevant to 'workplace conduct, safety, or security.' In practice, this exception is broad enough to encompass almost any disclosure made in a counseling session that touches on workplace relationships, management behavior, or the employee's feelings about their role. Mental health professionals who have left corporate employment and spoken to researchers describe an ongoing tension between their clinical ethics and their employment terms that most resolve by staying narrowly within the boundaries of what is formally protected.

The augmentation maintenance component of corporate healthcare is particularly consequential given the ubiquity of neural interfaces. Corporations that own the interface hardware their employees are using — which includes most Tier-1 employers, who issue standardized interface packages during induction — also own the maintenance and upgrade infrastructure for that hardware. Interface maintenance appointments are conducted at corporate facilities. The technicians performing them are corporate employees with full access to interface logs. Employees who attempt to seek interface maintenance outside the corporate system — whether for privacy reasons or because they are using non-standard augmentation — typically find that their corporate-issued interface is not compatible with external maintenance protocols, a restriction that is technically described as a 'security architecture feature.' The practical effect is that employees' most intimate technology is exclusively serviced by their employer.
